# Red-Teaming and System Evaluation {#sec-evaluating-agentic-architect}

![](images/ch10-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="Evaluation distinguishes the object, four judgments, a matched alternative, deliberate challenges, and a qualified claim that is not a commitment."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."
>
> — Marilyn Strathern, "'Improving Ratings': Audit in the British University System" (1997) [@Strathern1997Goodhart, p. 308]
:::

An AI-native design system can synthesize an appealing candidate architecture and still fail as an engineering workflow. Evaluation must establish whether the complete workflow delivers better architectural results, lower total cost at comparable quality, or both against a credible alternative. It must also test whether that advantage survives repetition, changed conditions, and deliberate adversarial stress.

This chapter separates the candidate design, individual components, configured technical system, and complete human-plus-technical workflow as evaluation objects. Matched comparisons establish workflow effects; controlled replacements test component contributions. Architecture outcomes, decision quality, total cost, and reliability remain distinct judgments, supported by cost records, repeated runs, benchmark audits, and red-team tests. The resulting claim states what is supported, contradicted, or unresolved within the tested scope. It informs a decision about tapeout or residual project risk without authorizing that decision.

## Architecture 2.0 Evaluation Objects

Validation of one object does not validate the others. A synthesized register-transfer level (RTL) module that passes its checks does not prove that a learned method caused the pass. Neither shows that the complete workflow saved engineering cost. When an automated synthesis loop produces an optimized floorplan, it is tempting to credit the generative model. Yet a simulated-annealing placer or a human-crafted verification wrapper may have determined the outcome, while the model supplied candidate seeds at substantial inference cost.

To build a fair comparison, we must first name the object each claim concerns.

1. **Candidate design.** The proposed microarchitecture, RTL netlist, configuration, script, mapping, or other design artifact. It is judged by its function, constraints, architectural quality, implementation feasibility, and the engineering effort required to integrate and maintain it.

2. **Method or component.** A single learned or conventional method, retriever, predictor, generator, optimizer, wrapper, checker, or other named module. Establishing its contribution requires a controlled replacement or ablation, a test that removes or swaps that specific part while holding the surrounding design system as fixed as the claim requires.

3. **Configured technical system.** The versioned combination of methods and components, represented design state, retrieval sources, routing rules, tool wrappers, automated checks, and stopping logic. It excludes human setup, intervention, review, repair, and decision-making.

4. **Complete human-plus-technical workflow.** The configured technical system alongside the architects, engineers, and reviewers who set up the task, intervene, interpret results, repair failures, approve changes, and decide when to stop.

These evaluation objects are independent of the operational layers in @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration. The layers describe the scope of automation and its authority over interfaces; the objects identify what a particular claim evaluates. For example, a point-assistance tool can be evaluated as a component, its generated RTL as a candidate design, and its use by an engineer as a complete workflow. A system-scale search likewise needs separate candidate, component, system, and workflow claims. Greater automation does not merge those claims or supply evidence for them.

### Freezing the System Under Test

Before measuring an advantage, we must name the evaluation object, freeze the relevant system identity, and define its permitted action space. The identity record, permitted actions, environment record, and evaluation protocol establish what the comparison holds fixed and what it varies. A benchmark score must be attached to the named object and the conditions under which it was evaluated. For a configured-system or complete-workflow claim, retry logic, retrieved material, prompts, and search policies form integral parts of the evaluated setup. Underlying models, tool access, feedback loops, and human-supplied wrappers materially change outcomes [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]. Naming only the model obscures the engineering system under test. Freezing its identity fixes the policies governing a run; it does not prevent design state, prompts, or retrieved material from evolving under those recorded policies.

The predefined legal action space determines what a score means and what failure modes can emerge during execution.

- **RTL or intermediate-representation generation.** The system produces a new design artifact. Evaluation covers functionality, blocking constraints, physical feasibility, structural integrity, and engineering maintenance effort.
- **Tool, script, or parameter tuning.** The system modifies analysis or implementation parameters. Evaluation must identify which settings may change, record their initial and selected values, and preserve the requirements, independent acceptance conditions, and declared stopping rules. Otherwise, modified test conditions can appear as engineering gains.
- **Microarchitecture change.** The system modifies CPU core structures, neural processing unit (NPU) tensor arrays, cache hierarchies, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) chiplet interfaces, or thermal throttling limits. Validating these changes across multi-tool environments (such as comparing RTL simulation in Verilator or Synopsys VCS against FireSim) requires evaluating affected workloads, software stacks, physical implementations, and integration consequences.
- **Test or constraint change.** The system modifies a testbench, formal property, timing constraint, or scoring script. Independent, evaluator-owned checks must verify that the system under test cannot weaken or bypass its own requirements.

This last action space needs a boundary before the experiment begins. Top-level requirements and final acceptance checks remain immutable and evaluator-owned. Internal design constraints may change when the legal action space permits them, but the system can only propose those changes for independent checking. A two-cycle arithmetic unit, for example, may need an internal multicycle timing exception backed by checks that its control logic really prevents capture on the intervening cycle. That proposal cannot lower the required clock frequency or waive the external interface contract. Freezing the evaluation therefore fixes both the requirements and the rule for admitting internal changes, rather than forbidding every change to a candidate's constraint file.

Pass rates for generated RTL, power, performance, and area (PPA) results from parameter tuning, and workload outcomes from microarchitecture changes represent distinct action spaces with different capabilities and attack surfaces. To interpret a comparison, the evaluation record must identify the features that can alter capabilities, costs, or interpretation (@tbl-complete-system-identity). Workflows using the same base model constitute different systems if they differ in retrieval sources, wrappers, retries, or tool access.

| **Element** | **What the record must identify** | **Why it matters** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Evaluation object** | Candidate design, method/component, configured technical system, or complete human-plus-technical workflow | Results can only be interpreted at the specific level evaluated. |
| **Learned components** | Immutable model snapshot or endpoint identity, access date, mutable alias if used, inference settings, and fine-tuning | Modifying models or settings creates a different system; aliases obscure exact runs. |
| **Design information** | Starting artifacts, retrieved sources with versions, represented state, retrieval coverage, conflict handling, and update policies | Extra or fresher information can explain apparent capability gains. |
| **Methods and instructions** | Selected generation, prediction, optimization, or other methods and their composition rules; system/task instructions; prompt policy; routing policy | Models are components in broader procedures; changing instructions or policies changes the evaluated setup. |
| **Legal action space** | Permitted design, tool, script, parameter, test, and constraint modifications | Allowed actions dictate supported claims and potential evaluation manipulation. |
| **System tool interfaces** | Tool wrappers/schemas, wrapper revision, available executable tools, and permitted calls | Interfaces determine possible actions and visible failures. |
| **Task and evaluation environments** | Task requirements and workloads; tool versions, configurations, checkpoints, dependencies, containers, and recorded outputs | Changed tasks or evaluation conditions can explain changed results. |
| **Checks** | Functional, architectural, physical, security, and acceptance checks; ownership and rules for admitting internal changes | Results are only as strong as cleared verification checks. |
| **Human work** | Setup, prompting, intervention, review, repair, and escalation roles | Hidden engineering effort makes automated results appear artificially cheap. |
| **Operating limits** | Compute, tool, time, retry, and review budgets plus stopping rules | Differences in budgets or access must be accounted for in the comparison. |
: **A complete-workflow identity extends well beyond the model.** The record distinguishes the evaluation object and renders every material source of capability and cost visible. {#tbl-complete-system-identity tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

Evaluations must retain the artifacts needed for reconstruction and use cryptographic hashes or immutable identifiers for prompts, retrieved snapshots, starting artifacts, scripts, constraints, workloads, containers, and raw records. A hash identifies an artifact but does not preserve its contents. The test of the record is replay. Every evaluated candidate must travel with the artifacts appropriate to its stage, such as synthesizable RTL or a simulator configuration, its parameter mapping, and the frozen tool configuration it ran under. These elements let a reviewer reconstruct the experiment and test whether the reported values recur. They do not eliminate stochastic tool variation, which the reliability analysis must measure separately. When immutable model snapshots are unavailable, record the endpoint identity and access dates, and state that these do not establish which immutable model state served the request. Exact replay cannot be assured from that record alone.

The eight Lighthouse domains discussed in @sec-intent-vs-spec, from workload to verification, help identify conditions that can alter an experiment. Record the relevant task and evaluation conditions separately; a change to one calls for checking which comparisons it affects. Separating system identity from environment identity avoids two common errors: falsely attributing environment capability to an underlying base model, and comparing percentages derived from different tasks, tool setups, or physical design stages.

### The Four Evaluation Judgments

No single metric establishes that an AI-native system improves architecture work. Compressing disparate engineering attributes into a single scalar score conceals critical trade-offs between physical correctness, tool coordination, compute expenditure, and empirical stability. Declared hard constraints must be met before other improvements can be weighed. An instructions-per-cycle (IPC) gain of $15\%$, for example, cannot compensate for a 250\ ps violation of a required hold-time bound at a receiving register.[^fn-hold-time-c10] The violation means the design has not established reliable operation under the checked conditions. Evaluation therefore separates four judgments so readers can see which engineering decisions a measurement supports and what remains unknown (@tbl-evaluation-metric-map).

| **Decision question** | **Concrete measures** | **Workflow insight** | **What metric cannot establish alone** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Is the architecture result supported?** | Function and blocking constraints; latency/throughput; power/thermal; area/cost; security; feasibility; maintainability; integration burden | Candidate achievement, requirements met, and verification depth | Whether AI improved engineering work, result repeatability, or commitment justification |
| **Did the workflow make sound decisions?** | Component selection; state consistency; tool/fidelity selection; interpretation accuracy; explanation faithfulness; decision usefulness; false accepts/rejects; escalation/recovery | Coordination quality, tool output interpretation, and evidence-backed decision making | Objective design adequacy, economic viability, or advantage stability under shift |
| **What was the total cost?** | Model tokens/calls; compiler builds; simulation, formal, and physical runs; compute/memory/licenses; setup/data; retries; elapsed time; human engineering | Resource expenditure and cost shifting | Candidate correctness or specific component attribution |
| **Is the advantage reliable?** | Repeated runs; calibration; worst cases; recovery; sensitivity to seeds, prompts, workloads, tools, and corners | Advantage recurrence rate and tested condition envelope | Structural reason for advantage or transferability beyond tested scope |
: **Evaluation metrics support distinct engineering decisions.** Architecture results take precedence; coordination, cost, and reliability explain how results were achieved. Red-team tests cut across all four rows. {#tbl-evaluation-metric-map tbl-colwidths="[22,30,22,26]"}

These rows are not interchangeable. Sound decisions can yield weak candidates in poor search spaces; strong candidates can mask inefficient workflows; and low total cost never compensates for blocking constraint violations. Explanation faithfulness tests whether explanations accurately reflect retained tool evidence. A stronger test asks whether the proposed mechanism predicts the direction of a change. A workload transposition or an aspect-ratio swap, for example, can test that prediction. If the result moves in the opposite direction, the proposed mechanism needs revision even when the explanation accurately cites the original measurements. Decision usefulness tests whether explanations assist human reviewers, and stability tests verify consistency under meaning-preserving syntax changes. None of these tests establishes architecture quality or operational cost on its own.

Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM)[^fn-helm-c10] established multi-scenario, multi-metric reporting for language models [@LiangEtAl2023HELM]. The four judgments apply that principle to architecture work. The proposed protocol in @sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol specifies fidelity stages appropriate to the claim, checks the system under test cannot edit, and matched accounting of human and machine cost on both arms. Its benchmark-integrity tests also examine trivial baselines and isolation between runs, which the benchmark-health section develops below. Component diagnostics (predictor calibration, generator diversity, optimizer regret) locate failures within the workflow but cannot substitute for architecture results or complete-workflow effects.

### Complete-Workflow Protocol {#sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol}

The following eight-step protocol is a proposed procedure for comparing an AI-native workflow with a conventional baseline. It fixes what is being compared, predeclares evaluation boundaries, and accounts for both successful and unsuccessful work. Candidate checks must reach the fidelity required by the claim: a simulator-level comparison need not establish physical signoff, while a physical implementation claim requires the relevant implementation checks.

1. Freeze both workflows alongside configured technical systems, environments, task populations, legal actions, evaluator-owned checks, and artifact identities.
2. Predeclare primary architecture outcomes, blocking constraints, design margins, resource envelopes, stopping rules, and failure treatments.
3. Balance or randomize paired tasks and human operators, isolating a held-out confirmation set from tuning.
4. Run both complete workflows, emitting execution records (@sec-execution-records) for every attempt on every assigned task.
5. Promote candidates through the fidelity stages required by the declared claim, auditing cheap screening proxies against independent stronger checks. For a physical implementation claim, such audits could test whether Pareto rankings survive dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) thermal throttling and voltage-drop ($IR$-drop) guardbands.[^fn-ir-drop-c10]
6. Estimate paired task-level outcome and cost differences with uncertainty quantification, including failures, censored runs, and task heterogeneity.
7. Execute declared sensitivity, component ablation, benchmark integrity, robustness, fault injection, and red-team tests under symmetric opportunities.
8. Report claims as supported, unsupported, or unresolved alongside governing tasks, conditions, costs, and limits.

For each reported metric, specify what is measured, the target population, the applicable evaluator-owned checks, the budget window, and the aggregation rules. For statistical estimates, also specify the experimental unit and uncertainty bounds. Four levels of activity must remain separate.

1. **Execution attempts:** individual efforts to fulfill an execution request, including retries and failed or interrupted work. An attempt may involve several backend jobs or end before a job starts. It may produce traces, measurements, or tool returns without producing a candidate.
2. **Generated candidates:** distinct artifacts or configurations proposed for a task. A candidate may undergo several checking attempts; those attempts do not each constitute a new candidate.
3. **Complete workflow runs:** full executions of the configured human-plus-technical workflow on an assigned task, potentially containing many attempts and candidates.
4. **Independent tasks or design decisions:** the units across which the study seeks to establish a workflow advantage. Repeated runs on one task measure variation within that task; they do not expand the number of independent tasks represented.

Dataset and observation records, such as traces, measurements, and tool returns, provide evidence about these activities; their number does not determine the number of independent replications. Treating nested seeds, attempts, candidates, or tool calls as independent task replications constitutes *pseudoreplication* [@Hurlbert1984Pseudoreplication].[^fn-pseudo-c10] In `pass@k`, sampling $k$ candidates estimates success probability on a single task, not $k$ independent tasks [@Chen2021Codex].

## The Architecture Result

An architectural evaluation begins with the result the study claims to establish. A simulator-level study can support a scoped comparison of cycle counts without claiming manufacturable silicon. A physical implementation claim must additionally clear the relevant implementation checks; workflow efficiency cannot compensate for failed equivalence checking or shorted power rails. At either scope, candidate designs must clear the functional invariants and blocking constraints required by that claim before secondary trade-offs become meaningful. A design that violates a required hold-time bound, deadlocks a coherence protocol, or exceeds the declared thermal limit fails that requirement, even if another metric improves.

Consider a generated RTL design that achieves high IPC in a simulator. Implementation under a 3\ nm process design kit (PDK) may expose routing congestion and negative slack that the simulator did not represent.[^fn-negative-slack-c10] An optimizer might also obtain a zero-slack report by silently excluding critical timing paths through spurious `set_false_path` exceptions in a Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file. The first case requires a stronger model of the candidate; the second requires checking that the evaluation still tests the required property. Both show why a reported score must remain tied to the checks that produced it.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Prioritize Soundness Over Tool Credit"}
**The principle:** Verify the candidate properties required by the stated architecture claim independently before crediting the design system with that result.

**The application:** Apply the same eligibility checks to both comparison arms, retain rejected candidates and their costs, and keep claims within the completed evaluation stage. A supported rejection or tie can be an architecture result; physical feasibility requires its own evidence.
:::

We separate eligibility criteria, core architectural objectives, implementation depth, and life cycle consequences. The examples below illustrate what each category can contain; the stated claim determines which checks and measurements apply.

- **Correctness and blocking constraints:** functional verification of instruction set architecture (ISA) contracts (RV64GCV), bus protocols (Advanced eXtensible Interface 5 (AXI5), UCIe), physical design rule checks (DRCs), and thermal limits (3\ W thermal design power (TDP)).
- **Architectural objectives:** workload throughput (XRBench, SPEC CPU2017, MLPerf), compiler fusion efficiency, vectorization overhead, interconnect energy per bit, and passive thermal dissipation.
- **Implementation feasibility:** deepest cleared tool stage, spanning gem5/Verilator simulation, Triton/Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) compilation, Yosys/Design Compiler synthesis, OpenROAD/Innovus place-and-route, OpenSTA/PrimeTime timing closure, and Yosys EQY / Cadence LEC equivalence checks under the process and library conditions declared for the study. For an illustrative 3\ nm-class low-power (LP) target, the available process data and tool support determine which of these checks can actually run.
- **Maintainability and future change cost:** code readability, interface clarity, design guideline adherence, and change cost under standard engineering change order (ECO) exercises.
- **Integration and verification burden:** bus protocol compliance, assertion clarity, and downstream verification debug overhead.

Implementation depth does not place all these tools and checks in a single sequence. Report which applicable checks passed and which remain unresolved: reaching place-and-route, for example, does not itself establish equivalence.

Report the underlying trade-offs through explicit Pareto fronts [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. If a weighted objective is used to select a design, disclose its weights and retain the separate outcomes so readers can inspect what that choice favors. Power and energy metrics must specify measurement windows, work completed, duty cycles, leakage states, and system boundaries, following the strict measurement discipline of MLPerf Power [@TschandEtAl2024MLPerfPower]. A local simulator victory does not settle implementation-facing readiness on its own.

## Coordination, Decision Quality, and Evidence Use

A supported architecture result establishes what the candidate comparison shows within its scope, but it does not explain how the system navigated the design space to reach it. AI-native workflows do more than generate candidate architectures; a well-designed workflow orchestrates the entire synthesis process by determining which component acts next, filtering the data that component receives, selecting the appropriate evaluation tool and simulation fidelity, integrating results back into the design state, and deciding whether sufficient evidence exists to halt or escalate to an architect. Even if every individual model or simulator functions correctly, the workflow can still fail if these decisions are coordinated poorly.

Evaluating these systems requires reconstructing the sequence of consequential architecture decisions. For every such step in the pipeline, the study record must preserve the core design question, the available state, the chosen action, the expected architectural observation, the actual result returned, the applied interpretation, and the subsequent decision. Preserving this audit trail does not require hoarding every internal token or private large language model (LLM) chain of thought; the goal is retaining the engineering context needed to explain why the workflow modified a design or reached a specific conclusion.

Reconstructing these decision paths exposes six failure modes during automated architecture synthesis.

1. **Role-selection failures** occur when the system invokes a generative model where a deterministic lookup, hardware predictor, classical optimizer, formal equivalence check, or direct human decision was required.
2. **State failures** occur when the wrapper drops, duplicates, or misattributes design constraints, candidate identities, tool statuses, physical units, or prior simulation results to the wrong microarchitecture.
3. **Information-use failures** arise when retrieval mechanisms omit decision-relevant documentation, fetch an outdated intellectual property (IP) version, mask conflicting data sources, or return material that fails to support the downstream architectural claim.
4. **Tool-selection failures** occur when the workflow deploys an unsuitable simulation fidelity or repeats an uninformative run. For example, a 48-hour gate-level simulation in Synopsys VCS or Cadence Xcelium may be unnecessary if a fast analytical model or a Verilator trace already exposes a tile-buffer throughput bottleneck. That trace can establish behavior represented in the RTL model; routability still requires physical-design evidence.
5. **Interpretation failures** emerge when a tool call completes successfully, yet the workflow misreads performance metrics, incorrectly treats an inconclusive timing check as a pass, or misattributes an IPC gain to the wrong hardware mechanism.
6. **Control failures** trigger when the system should halt, escalate, roll back a configuration, or request human review, but instead pushes forward or commits a broken design state.

Distinguishing tool execution, architectural observation, and decision support avoids a common counting error in evaluation. A completed tool call does not guarantee a useful architectural observation, and a useful observation does not guarantee a supported design decision. Evaluation protocols must explicitly report all three stages: tracking false accepts (where the workflow improperly advances an invalid candidate) alongside false rejects (where it prematurely discards a candidate that independent checks later establish as viable within the stated scope). Parser failures, stale cache data, incomplete traces, and corrupted state transitions belong in the same record because they directly pollute the information available to subsequent steps.

Assessing tool-using behavior requires reporting structured rates rather than a single aggregate score. Protocols should record valid and authorized tool invocations, the yield of useful architectural observations per call, and first-attempt versus retry success rates categorized by failure class. The audit record must also track redundant actions, unsupported retries, adherence to stopping rules, escalation accuracy on evaluator-defined edge cases, intervention-free synthesis completions, human takeovers, and state recovery reliability. A retry following a transient electronic design automation (EDA) license timeout differs from an iterative attempt to repair a conceptual flaw in a cache hierarchy; raw aggregate retry counts remain secondary to root-cause classifications. Relating observation yield to compute cost also requires the resource accounting developed in the following sections.

These rates must be evaluated against declared opportunity sets: measuring stop-rule compliance exclusively over runs that hit a stopping condition, evaluating escalation accuracy solely on pre-tagged test cases, calculating intervention-free completion and human takeover metrics for tasks eligible under the declared operating mode, and tracking recovery success only where protocols demand restoration to a trusted golden state.

Retrieved design information equally demands positive quality metrics: logging the identity and exact version of each specification or IP source, assessing coverage of facts relevant to the architectural decision, and flagging unresolved data conflicts. The evaluation must verify whether retrieved material supports the specific design claims made in downstream steps. While an ablation study might show that retrieval altered the final layout or microarchitecture outcome, it cannot establish whether fetched information was current, comprehensive, or correctly applied.

Decision quality must be benchmarked against formally declared expected actions or, where possible, through independent engineering reviews. When architectural decisions remain ambiguous, reports should document inter-reviewer agreement and unresolved design alternatives rather than manufacturing a single artificial label. For narrower predictive tasks, statistical and machine-learning evaluations offer three tools: confidence calibration, strictly proper scoring rules, and risk-coverage curves. Consider a predeclared binary outcome, such as whether an accelerator candidate passes a strict, evaluator-owned timing check within a fixed evaluation budget. Among held-out designs assigned $80\%$ confidence, about $80\%$ should reach that specific outcome under tested conditions if those predictions are calibrated [@GuoEtAl2017Calibration]. A strictly proper scoring rule is maximized in expectation only when the forecaster reports its true probability distribution [@GneitingRaftery2007ScoringRules]. Risk-coverage curves show how error rates among cases handled without abstention or escalation change as the system handles a larger fraction of eligible cases [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification]. If a workflow lacks built-in probability estimates, its ability to abstain or escalate should be evaluated directly rather than inventing a synthetic confidence measure. While these statistical tools assess reported uncertainty and selective handling over fixed horizons, they cannot validate candidate functionality, physical feasibility, or the value of the resulting computer architecture.

Human support is part of the workflow being evaluated. If a senior verification engineer spends forty hours patching broken decoder logic, revising SDC constraints, and triaging memory-consistency violations generated by an automated tool, a claim of "autonomous synthesis" omits work needed to obtain the result. Studies must record where engineers supplied missing architectural context, corrected flawed interpretations, manually overrode routing decisions, repaired broken artifacts, or terminated divergent runs. Core decision-quality metrics include the fraction of decisions requiring human support, manual override rates, post-intervention recovery rates, and the architectural outcome following an override. The record should connect each intervention to the evidence available before it and the decision reached afterward. Total time to reach a supported decision belongs in the accompanying cost account. Together, the decision record and cost account can reveal whether the workflow reduced engineering work or shifted it into developing prompts, resolving SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) violations, drafting ECOs, and correcting unroutable pin placements.

## Total Design Cost Accounting

A local speedup does not establish a complete-workflow efficiency gain: savings may be offset by later checking and repair. Total-cost accounting must include every attempt, including failed and retried work. Human effort, model compute, tool usage, licenses, energy consumption, and elapsed time should be reported separately; combining them requires a disclosed conversion rule appropriate to the comparison. One-time setup and training overhead must be separated from per-task costs, and active service demand must be distinguished from queueing and schedule delays. A surrogate fitted for one project, a wrapper written for one tool path, and a framework built for one study all incur costs that must be accounted for over a declared reuse horizon. An approach that repays itself across hundreds of candidate evaluations can lose decisively to a conventional method on a program that requires only a dozen. The following subsections develop the attempt records and amortization calculations needed to make that comparison. Matched comparisons relate total cost directly to a supported architecture outcome or to the total budget required to reach a predeclared outcome threshold.

Consider the full cost of an architectural decision. An architect does not merely tally the final synthesis run; the accounting must encompass the weeks of engineering time spent debugging failed testbenches, the cloud compute expenditures for thousands of discarded exploration episodes, and the EDA license tokens locked up during overnight simulations. When evaluating an AI-native workflow, comparing only the final successful model inference against a senior engineer's entire work week is a severe accounting failure.

To establish efficiency, we must track resources consumed from task assignment through the declared endpoint of the comparison, whether that endpoint is a simulator-backed recommendation, rejection, or physical signoff. The account must also include the share of earlier setup, training, and data preparation charged to the comparison. Expected future change and ECO costs should be reported separately from observed expenditure, with their scenario assumptions stated. The cost classes in @tbl-total-system-cost show why model token counts alone cannot establish total architectural expense.

| **Cost class** | **Examples to record** |
| --- | --- |
| **Human setup** | Formulation, artifact preparation, environment integration, prompt and procedure development |
| **Human operation** | Supervision, intervention, failure triage, and manual design work |
| **Human review and decision work** | Independent checking, design review, documentation, approval preparation, and unresolved follow-up |
| **Model and general compute** | Model calls and tokens, inference time, accelerator time, training or adaptation, memory, storage, energy, and orchestration |
| **Engineering tools** | Compiler builds; invocations by tool type, fidelity, and status; simulation runs and cycles; formal, synthesis, physical, field-programmable gate array (FPGA) / emulation, and lab measurements; license peak concurrency limits, token checkout duration, queue denial wait latency, and backoff throttling |
| **Data and samples** | Workload traces, training/adaptation data, reference outputs, implementation samples, and silicon measurements |
| **Verification and integration** | Check development, proof and simulation work, debug, interface and software integration, regressions, and closing evidence |
| **Future change and ECO work** | Expected design edits, affected modules/interfaces, verification reruns, implementation work, and review for declared scenarios |
| **Failure and recovery** | Invalid candidates, repeated runs, rollback, restored state, debugging, and rework |
| **Schedule** | Wall-clock time, time to a supported decision, critical-path delay, and completion-time variability |
: **Total cost includes all work performed before, during, and after automated search within the declared accounting boundary.** Categories must be reported separately unless a disclosed accounting rule converts them into a common, justified unit. {#tbl-total-system-cost tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

Selective reporting of only the accelerator-hours consumed by the final successful run omits the human setup time, the debug effort, and the failed iterations that constrain engineering throughput. Including those costs makes it possible to assess whether faster candidate production reduces the total work needed to reach a supported decision.

### Execution Records and Candidate Flow

Reconstructing costs requires a record of every attempt, linked to its workflow run, candidate, configuration, and random seed where applicable. Every attempt carries an execution status (completed, crashed, timed out, canceled, license unavailable) and an engineering outcome (passed, violated, infeasible, inconclusive, or unreached). Partial outputs, allocated timeouts, and consumed hardware resources must be preserved. A timeout followed by a retry constitutes two distinct attempts, not two independent configurations; @sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol establishes these experimental-unit distinctions.

Tracking resources for each attempt separates the cost of searching the design space from the cost of fragile infrastructure. The per-attempt cost record extends the execution record with the comparison arm, evaluation stage, resource use, and linked human work (@tbl-attempt-cost-record). Failed attempts, tool crashes, and manual repair sessions therefore remain part of the comparison even when they produce no finalist. Execution status alone does not determine censoring: the record must identify which measurement, if any, remains censored and why. A timed-out attempt, for example, has observed resource consumption even when its time to completion remains unknown.

| **Evaluation attribute group** | **Attributes added or made explicit for comparison** |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Comparison placement** | Comparison arm, paired task, workflow-run/candidate/configuration/attempt identifiers, random seed where applicable, evaluator-owned stage/fidelity, and promotion status |
| **Engineering outcome** | Passed, violated, infeasible, inconclusive, or unreached; coverage, waiver status, and deepest evidence stage |
| **Execution, censoring, and disposition** | Completed, crashed, timed out, canceled, or license unavailable; allocated timeout; censored measurement and reason, if any; partial output; and inclusion rules |
| **Resources and cost** | Model/tool calls; core-hours, accelerator-hours, peak memory, storage, network, energy, license occupancy duration and peak concurrency, queue wait latency, backoff throttling status, retries, and recovery |
| **Recovery and state** | State invalidated/restored, preserved descendants, and checkpoint lineage |
| **Human-work linkage** | Active engineering minutes by role, independent review, intervention, and waiting linked to affected attempts |
: **Evaluation records extend operational tracking across all attempts.** Capturing outcomes, censoring, resource consumption, and linked human effort across all attempts prevents artificial cost erasure from finalist-only reporting. {#tbl-attempt-cost-record tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

### Resource Vectors and Amortization

Expert review hours, accelerator-hours, EDA license-hours, and schedule delays represent distinct resources that cannot be collapsed without explicit conversion models. Report these costs as a multidimensional resource vector; when computing monetary totals, disclose the currency, base year, and price sources. Separate intrinsic service demand (active compute, memory, tool execution, license occupancy) from realized schedule latency (including queue delays, license denials, and scheduler preemptions). Parallel execution may shorten elapsed time without reducing total compute-hours, while a license queue may lengthen elapsed time without adding active tool execution. Both resource use and time to completion matter, but they answer different questions.

Keep observed study costs, one-time integration/training overhead, and projected downstream life-cycle costs separately identifiable. Declare the expected amortization horizon and apply the same accounting rules to both comparison arms. For an additive resource such as engineering hours, a fixed setup cost of $F$ spread across $N$ uses contributes $F/N$ per use, in addition to the work required for that use. Report the fixed cost and assumed number of uses alongside the amortized value; a projected reuse horizon does not establish realized savings. If future reuse is uncertain, show how the comparison changes across plausible horizons. Peak memory and peak license concurrency require separate reporting rather than this additive calculation.

Record product quality attributes (verification depth, maintainability, ECO burden) separately from workflow resource expenditures. For example, an estimate of future ECO burden is a product assessment, whereas engineering hours actually spent on an ECO belong in the cost record. Link the records so that the same work is not charged twice. Similarly, include setup work once in the total over the declared horizon, or allocate it across uses; do not add both the full setup cost and its amortized shares to that total.

Total-cost records support two distinct efficiency claims: complete workflow efficiency (relating supported outcomes to total resource budgets) and sample efficiency (measuring supported improvement per observation at a specific fidelity). A method may need fewer observations yet incur more total cost through training, proposal generation, checking, or human review. State which observations enter the sample-efficiency denominator and retain the other expenditures in the complete-workflow comparison. Both measures require isolating stochastic variance to avoid spurious efficiency claims [@BouthillierEtAl2021UnreproducibleML; @HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL].

### Candidate Flow and Funnels

Candidate identity is tracked by declared design meaning rather than job identifiers. Semantic repairs create child candidates linked to parent designs, whereas mechanical retries (after license stalls or state recovery) retain the original candidate identity and log a new attempt. This distinction lets architects separate exploration of new designs from repeated execution of existing ones. Parent–child links also distinguish repair from independent proposals; a count of unique candidates alone does not measure the breadth of exploration.

Reporting only the finalist erases the attrition and costs at every stage before it. Grouping attempts by candidate identity yields a per-arm candidate funnel (@tbl-candidate-funnel). Count each candidate once at each stage it reaches, while retaining the costs of all its attempts. The funnel shows where candidates leave the process; linked outcomes explain whether they violated a constraint, were not selected for promotion, or could not complete a check. These are different reasons for attrition, with different implications for the design and the workflow. If a stage has a zero denominator, report the count and mark its fraction undefined rather than recording a zero rate.

| **Funnel stage** | **Count and fractions to report per arm** | **Required denominators** | **Linked attrition and cost accounting** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Unique candidates proposed** | Count $U$; starting fraction $U/U$ | All unique candidates proposed or supplied to the arm | Proposal cost, duplicate attempts, and candidates censored before eligibility review |
| **Low-fidelity eligibility** | Count $E$; $E/U$ | All unique candidates proposed | Eligibility outcome, attrition reason, stage cost, retries, and censoring |
| **Promoted or finalist** | Count $P$; $P/E$ and $P/U$ | Eligible candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Promotion rule, nonpromotion reasons, selection cost, ties, and retries |
| **Higher-fidelity completion** | Count $H$; $H/P$ and $H/U$ | Promoted candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Completed check identity, noncompletion reasons, stage cost, timeouts, and infrastructure failures |
| **Blocking-check pass** | Count $B$; $B/H$ and $B/U$ | Higher-fidelity completions and all unique candidates proposed | Blocking-check identity, pass/violation/waiver status, stage cost, and retries |
| **Final comparison and selection** | Counts $C$ compared, $S$ selected; $C/B$, $S/C$, $S/U$ | Blocking-check passes, final comparison set, and all unique candidates proposed | Comparison/selection rule, dominated/unselected reasons, final-stage cost, and declared no-selection outcomes |
: **Candidate funnels expose stage-by-stage attrition and resource consumption.** Counts, fractions, denominators, reasons, retries, censoring events, and stage costs remain connected to attempt lineage rather than reported only for finalists. {#tbl-candidate-funnel tbl-colwidths="[22,26,24,28]"}

In an illustrative exploratory study starting with $U = 1{,}000$ proposed candidate architectures, $E=200$ survive static syntax and area screening ($E/U=20\%$), and $P=50$ clear analytical throughput thresholds to earn promotion ($P/E=25\%$). Suppose $H=20$ complete the declared higher-fidelity sequence of cycle-accurate gem5 simulation, synthesis, and place-and-route without timing out ($H/P=40\%$). Of those implementations, $B=5$ pass blocking DRC and static timing checks ($B/H=25\%$). All five enter the final comparison ($C=5$), and $S=1$ is selected for the next integration stage ($S/C=20\%$, representing an end-to-end yield of $S/U = 0.1\%$). Reporting only the single finalist ($S=1$) erases the compute cost and engineering effort spent on the other 999 candidates.

Aggregate stage costs from the linked attempt records, counting shared human work episodes only once across affected attempts. Retain the stage reached, check identity, outcome category, total cost, coverage, and waivers alongside the funnel counts. Analytical estimates, simulations, formal proofs, equivalence checks, synthesis runs, physical implementations, and hardware measurements remain distinct observation classes, each with its own costs and claim scopes (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).
### Cost-Quality Frontiers

In physical design, inexpensive learned estimates can substitute for expensive downstream analysis [@Kahng2018Machine]. Deploying upfront computation is economical if it prevents failed tool runs, but this trade-off must be measured empirically. Reporting design quality as a function of total cost identifies nondominated points on the cost-quality frontier (@fig-cost-quality-frontier).

```{python}
#| label: fig-cost-quality-frontier
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A cost-quality frontier keeps one declared architecture outcome and one disclosed cost measure visible together.** In this illustrative construction [@Kahng2018Machine], normalized architectural outcome (y-axis) is plotted against a synthetic cost index (x-axis). Filled blue points trace the nondominated Pareto frontier of efficient workflows, while faded gray points indicate dominated configurations that incur excess cost without outcome gains. The red dashed horizontal line marks a predeclared quality threshold ($0.78$), identifying the lowest-cost workflow that delivers a defensible result. Values are constructed for illustration.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Illustrative scatter plot of total workflow cost against one normalized, predeclared architecture outcome. Four filled points form an increasing nondominated frontier, three faded points are dominated, and a horizontal dashed line marks the predeclared outcome threshold."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
import numpy as np

apply_style()

# Constructed illustrative parameters: the frontier and dominated points below are
# author-chosen to show what Pareto dominance looks like on a cost-quality plane, not measured. Former label: Frontier y(c) = 0.52 + 0.38 * (1 - exp(-0.75 * (c - 0.8))) derived from physical design multi-objective Pareto formulations (Kahng, 2018).
costs_frontier = [1.0, 1.8, 3.2, 4.8]
outcomes_frontier = [0.58, 0.72, 0.85, 0.89]

costs_dominated = [2.2, 3.6, 4.5]
outcomes_dominated = [0.63, 0.74, 0.81]

threshold = 0.78

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.12))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

c_smooth = np.linspace(0.8, 5.2, 100)
y_smooth = 0.52 + 0.38 * (1 - np.exp(-0.75 * (c_smooth - 0.8)))
ax.plot(
    c_smooth,
    y_smooth,
    color=COLORS["blue"],
    linewidth=1.2,
    linestyle="--",
    alpha=0.6,
    zorder=1,
)

ax.scatter(
    costs_frontier,
    outcomes_frontier,
    color=COLORS["blue"],
    s=36,
    zorder=3,
    label="Nondominated workflows (frontier)",
)

ax.scatter(
    costs_dominated,
    outcomes_dominated,
    color=COLORS["muted"],
    alpha=0.6,
    s=28,
    zorder=2,
    label="Dominated workflows",
)

ax.axhline(
    threshold,
    color=COLORS["red"],
    linewidth=1.0,
    linestyle=":",
    zorder=1,
    label=f"Outcome threshold ({threshold})",
)

ax.annotate(
    "minimum cost to\nreach threshold",
    xy=(3.2, threshold),
    xytext=(3.5, 0.65),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], lw=0.8),
    fontsize=6,
    color=COLORS["ink"],
)

ax.set_xlabel("Total workflow cost index (normalized)", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Supported architecture outcome (normalized)", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_xlim(0.6, 5.6)
ax.set_ylim(0.4, 0.96)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, loc="lower right")
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

Nondominated frontiers identify efficient choices among the measured workflows, while dominated points reveal excess expenditure without outcome gains under the declared cost rule. In this constructed example, the least expensive sampled point above the quality threshold is the candidate to investigate. The smooth curve does not establish an attainable cost between sampled points, and the synthetic index is not a measured dollar cost. A practical comparison must supply those measurements before selecting a workflow.

Establishing a cost-quality frontier for an AI-native system quantifies how its internal efficiency scales, but demonstrating that this frontier represents an advantage demands testing it against an external competitor under matched conditions.

## Matched Baseline and Candidate Comparisons

A claim of workflow advantage requires a credible external baseline. An isolated performance delta or absolute synthesis score does not show whether an AI-native workflow improves on a competitive alternative. Consider a heavily tuned, prompt-engineered AI search loop compared with an untuned commercial EDA default or a naive random search. If the AI loop receives hundreds of exploration iterations while the conventional baseline receives a single shot, a better result could reflect unequal tuning opportunities rather than a workflow advantage. The comparison must make those opportunities and their costs visible. Choosing an alternative appropriate to the claim and establishing matched conditions are therefore part of the evaluation itself.

### Matching Protocols and Comparator Baselines

Evaluating a program adoption claim asks whether the complete workflow improves supported architecture outcomes or lowers total cost relative to the strongest practical alternative across declared tasks, conditions, budgets, and checks. Answering this question requires matching complete workflows across architecture questions, starting artifacts, source and tool access, evaluator-owned checks, cost rules, budgets, and stopping rules.

Distinct comparison arms test different hypotheses: random search tests whether guided search exceeds unguided sampling under matched budgets; point AI versus conventional workflows tests whether point assistance advances current practice; and comparisons among no-AI, retrieval-only, foundation-model, and full AI-native configurations test how their supported outcomes and total costs differ. These configurations need not form a progression of increasing capability. Random search can serve as a diagnostic floor, but whether it is also a credible practical alternative depends on the architecture question. Other practical comparators include direct enumeration, deterministic heuristics, commercial optimizers, established EDA flows, or human-directed studies (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

Matching the dimensions in @tbl-matched-system-comparison reduces alternative explanations for a measured gain. Differences that cannot be matched must remain explicit limits on the comparison.

| **Comparison element** | **Matching rule** |
| --- | --- |
| **Evaluation object** | Compare complete workflows for adoption estimates; reserve components for controlled ablations. |
| **Architecture question** | Require both workflows to resolve the same design decision under matched conditions; retain the identities of the distinct candidates each produces. |
| **Starting information** | Provide identical specifications, artifacts, workload info, prior results, and source access. |
| **Development and tuning** | Grant comparable opportunity, expertise, and budget for prompt, heuristic, and workflow tuning. |
| **Evaluation tools and checks** | Provide identical evaluator-run tools and stages, judged by identical evaluator-owned checks. |
| **Budget** | Enforce a single cost-accounting window across declared human, machine, tool, review, and time budgets. |
| **Human capability** | Deploy practitioners with matched task expertise in both arms and record specific actions. |
| **Human-judged outcomes** | Conceal arm identities and randomize review order wherever artifacts permit. |
| **Stopping rule** | Apply identical success, failure, exhaustion, and timeout conditions across both arms. |
| **Reporting** | Publish symmetric architecture outcomes, failed runs, costs, and uncertainty profiles. |
: **A matched comparison holds the architecture task and evidence standard fixed.** Matching reduces alternative explanations; remaining differences limit the resulting estimate of complete-workflow effects. {#tbl-matched-system-comparison tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

A matched evaluation assigns a single declared architecture question and evaluator-owned evidence standard to parallel arms: the AI-native workflow and the strongest practical alternative (@fig-matched-complete-systems). Identical starting artifacts, source access, shared evaluation tools, evaluator-owned checks, budget windows, and stopping rules make the resulting difference interpretable as an estimate of the complete-workflow effect, subject to the remaining matching assumptions.

![**Matched complete-system workflows estimate the effect of adopting an AI-native design workflow.** A single declared architecture study feeds in parallel into the AI-native workflow and the strongest practical alternative under identical starting artifacts, source access, shared evaluation tools, evaluator-owned checks, budget windows, and stopping rules. Task-paired differences in supported outcomes and total resource costs estimate the complete-workflow effect within the tested envelope; they do not isolate individual component contributions.](images/fig-matched-complete-systems){#fig-matched-complete-systems
fig-alt="One declared architecture study feeds an AI-native complete human-plus-technical workflow and the strongest practical complete workflow. The comparison fixes the architecture question, starting artifacts and source access, shared evaluation tools, evaluator-owned acceptance checks, conditions, cost-accounting window, budgets, stopping rules, and reporting requirements. Each workflow returns a supported architecture outcome or declared failure, stated limits, a resource-cost record, and results across repeated runs and varied conditions. Failed runs remain part of the reported results. Task-paired differences estimate the effect of adopting the whole AI-native workflow conditional on matching assumptions and the tested envelope. They do not isolate a component or AI contribution."
width="80%"}

Measuring task-paired differences in supported outcomes and total consumed resources estimates complete-workflow impact across repeated runs and varied conditions. This estimate is tightly bounded by matching assumptions and the tested envelope; isolating specific component contributions requires controlled replacements (@sec-locating-component-contribution).

Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) analysis provides a concrete example of why the comparison context belongs with the result [@JouppiEtAl2017TPU]. Its throughput and performance-per-watt claims identify datacenter baselines and workloads, with memory and compute bounds helping explain the outcomes. In an automated search study, the analogous context also includes the opportunities each workflow had to tune itself before confirmation.

### Predeclaration and the Confirmation Firewall

Long before either arm executes a single run, we must predeclare primary architecture outcomes, required task and condition coverage, acceptable total-cost envelopes, and minimum thresholds for worthwhile architecture improvement and cost reduction. We also establish a strict limit on maximum acceptable quality loss and specify the number of paired tasks and statistical repeats required to distinguish those margins with confidence. Without these rules, post hoc analysis risks retroactively classifying imperceptible gains as successful or justifying cheaper results when architecture quality has degraded.

Task population and sampling rules belong in the study plan. First, name the exact class of architecture decisions the program claim covers. Then, define how tasks, workloads, implementation conditions, and repeats are sampled from that class. Adaptive prompt development, method tuning, and search heuristic exploration remain confined to a designated development set. Primary program comparisons insist on held-out tasks and conditions that never influenced design choices, followed by evaluator-owned confirmation of any selected architecture result.

A strict firewall separates exploratory configuration development from confirmatory evaluation [@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]. The record states how many prompts, models, routing policies, metrics, task variants, and analysis techniques were evaluated before settling on the final comparison. The primary outcome and target analysis are named before inspecting the holdout set. If adaptive searching across configurations or outcomes could plausibly explain a reported advantage, a fresh confirmation set is required rather than treating the best-selected result as confirmatory [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. This same development opportunity and accounting rule apply to the strongest practical alternative. If a mature baseline carries decades of inherited tuning, the study records that historic advantage rather than tuning only the AI-native arm and declaring the contest matched.

When human engineers direct either arm, tasks are assigned using a predeclared balancing or randomization rule, logging who worked on which task. If the same architect operates both systems, tool order is rotated to account for cognitive carryover. If different engineering teams are deployed, their experience is matched and remaining skill gaps are reported. Both arms receive a declared familiarization period and stable operating procedure, separating setup time from measured task duration. If exposure to the first arm reveals critical design insights that would advantage the second, fresh tasks, a washout period, or carryover modeling must be applied.

When outcomes are human-judged (such as hardware maintainability or explanation quality), arm labels are concealed and review order is randomized wherever feasible. When generated artifacts reveal their origin through distinct coding styles or structural quirks, the study records leaked cues, unblinded judgments, reviewer agreement rates, and final adjudication procedures.

Every assigned run must remain in the final result pool. If a run yields an incomplete design, triggers a timeout, suffers a tool failure, or exhausts its compute budget, it retains its declared result status and resource cost. Failed runs must never quietly disappear because they failed to produce a final benchmark score. While results restricted to successful runs provide an optimistic secondary view, they cannot replace the all-assigned comparison upon which the program claim depends.

A timeout is treated as a failure when the targeted outcome is success within a fixed budget. However, it is treated as a right-censored event when the outcome metric is the time required to reach a supported result; the completion time is known only to exceed the timeout threshold (@sec-data-representations-world-models) [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. The analysis must not discard either case or assign fabricated completion times to simplify the math.

The cost-quality comparison from @fig-cost-quality-frontier applies to both arms across predeclared budget milestones. As human effort, model compute, tool utilization, and wall-clock time increase, the report tracks the best supported architecture outcome alongside the total cost required to reach the declared quality threshold, enforcing declared resource envelopes or conversion rules.

## Ablation and Component Attribution {#sec-locating-component-contribution}

Comparing an AI-native workflow with the strongest practical alternative estimates the effect of adopting the entire workflow. It does not identify which workflow component or method drove a gain. Controlled replacements and ablations test that dependence by swapping or removing one element while holding surrounding components, human procedures, task definitions, verification checks, and resource budgets fixed. The substitutions in @tbl-system-ablations ask which parts the result depends on; they do not assume that component contributions add independently.

| **Component under test** | **Useful comparison** | **Claim the comparison can support** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete AI-native workflow | Compare with the strongest practical alternative workflow under the same task, evidence standard, and total-cost accounting | The effect of adopting the whole workflow on result quality or cost, not an isolated AI contribution |
| Foundation model | Replace it with retrieval-only assistance, a smaller model, or another declared model while preserving the surrounding workflow | Whether the measured result depends on that model capability and its cost |
| Generation | Replace generated candidates with the same-size human, rule-based, or existing candidate set | Whether generation changed candidate quality or diversity at the declared cost |
| Prediction | Remove the learned screen or replace it with a conventional proxy and send a matched sample to the higher-fidelity check | Whether prediction saved evaluation work without discarding decisive candidates |
| Optimization | Replace the search policy with the strongest practical conventional method at matched budgets | Whether the optimizer improved the cost-quality relationship |
| Retrieved design information | Remove, freeze, or substitute the retrieval source while preserving the remaining system; check source versions, decision-relevant coverage, conflicts, and local claim support | Whether retrieved material changed results and which source dependencies remain |
| Routing and role selection | Replace adaptive routing with a fixed sequence or evaluator-declared component choice | Whether dynamic method and tool selection improved decisions or merely added complexity |
| Tool feedback | Restrict or delay selected feedback attributes while keeping tool stages fixed | Which returned information enables correction and which merely adds cost |
| Automated checking | Replace one checker with an independently developed check where feasible | Whether the conclusion depends on one checker or one shared assumption |
| Human intervention | Compare declared intervention policies and record every intervention | How much human work is necessary for the measured result |
: **Ablations locate dependencies inside a complete workflow.** They do not turn an interacting system architecture into a set of independent, additive contributions. {#tbl-system-ablations tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

Evaluating the quality of a new architectural method requires equalizing tool budgets, whereas measuring the end-to-end efficiency of the complete workflow allows budgets to vary, provided every resource spent is accounted for. Any claim remains bounded to the specific component or entire workflow modified in the comparison. One-at-a-time replacements do not guarantee causal isolation because workflow components interact: a learned surrogate may appear effective only when paired with a specific simulated-annealing optimizer, or a foundation model might seem highly capable only because a human engineer catches its out-of-distribution errors before they reach Innovus. We begin by isolating the components most likely to drive observed performance gains, test targeted interactions when initial conclusions shift, and report coupled dependencies that cannot be separated. When interactions prevent attribution, the individual component's contribution remains unresolved.

Across large design spaces where dozens of components interact, preregistered fractional-factorial experiments screen a balanced subset of configurations without requiring exhaustive enumeration. Plackett–Burman designs provide an efficient first-pass screen of main effects [@PlackettBurman1946Design], followed by targeted designs to untangle specific, high-value interactions. Even promising component combinations demand held-out confirmation against evaluator-owned architectural benchmarks. These screens can confound main effects with interactions, so an apparent component benefit may depend on which other components were present. Untested or inseparable interactions remain unresolved.

## Reliability of the Advantage

An estimated outcome and cost difference does not guarantee a reliable architectural advantage. Repeated runs test whether an effect recurs on the same task, while varied conditions test whether the advantage survives practical shifts in hardware decisions. A claim of a reliable advantage needs both forms of evidence; a single stochastic run supplies a measurement without establishing its repeatability [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL].

Reliability requires more than an acceptable average success rate. A reliability report covers worst-case scenarios, blocking constraint violations, and recovery mechanisms after failure, quantifying the time and human effort required for recovery alongside the fraction of automated decisions overridden by experts. Confidence levels must calibrate with eventual architectural results: a workflow that is correct $90\%$ of the time but expresses maximum confidence during its failures presents a worse risk profile than one with the same pass rate and properly calibrated uncertainty estimates.

Numerical architecture estimates demand their own calibration records, reporting interval coverage, interval sharpness (ensuring narrowness without sacrificing coverage), and errors near decision boundaries [@GneitingRaftery2007ScoringRules, pp. 369, 374], tied to specific tool stages, time horizons, and condition distributions. Calibration on one workload, process node, design family, or toolchain does not hold once conditions shift [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift]. Changing any of these factors introduces a new target condition requiring remeasurement of interval coverage and error. This testing qualifies predictor uncertainty under that newly defined condition; it does not prove that the proposed architecture is functionally correct or physically feasible.

### System and Apparatus Variance

Evaluations must carefully pair comparison arms across tasks, controlled tool factors, and declared starting conditions. Changes to model or search seeds represent repeated runs under a single, fixed system configuration. Conversely, a changed prompt represents an altered system configuration unless a predeclared prompt-sampling policy is defined as part of the system under test. None of these variations constitute an independent architecture task. Repeated runs are also where the generator's own dispersion is measured, since a single proposal that happened to win says nothing about the distribution it was drawn from. Two measures separate a search from a lucky draw: the fraction of proposals across repeated samplings that are unique legal configurations rather than duplicates, and whether a meaning-preserving rewording of the prompt preserves the candidate ranking. The array record of @sec-running-the-loop, holding one model call, supports neither. Data analysis must report successes, failures, constraint violations, recoveries, medians, interquartile ranges, and granular per-task results. Relying solely on means and standard deviations hides the bimodal outcomes hardware studies routinely produce, where one cluster of runs fails implementation while another finds a strong design.

The evaluation apparatus itself introduces another layer of variability. Subtle shifts in placement seeds and tool settings alter physical-design fit [@Altera2026QuartusFitter], while supposedly neutral build or environment adjustments perturb measured performance [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. The relevant dispersion must be measured on the designs and tool flow used in the comparison. For a hypothetical $4\%$ area improvement, paired reruns test how much of the apparent gain persists across placement seeds. Ensuring nominally fixed setups are repeatable requires conducting identical reruns, followed by separate sensitivity studies that deliberately vary specific factors. Environmental variance must never be subtracted from model variance under the false assumption that they are independent. The comparison must predeclare exactly what it estimates: an average across declared apparatus factors, a result frozen at one specific setup, or a true worst-case scenario. When system differences cannot be distinguished from apparatus noise at required practical margins, the architectural result remains unresolved.

The number of paired seeds a claimed gain needs follows from that dispersion rather than from convention. Let $\sigma_d$ be the standard deviation of the per-seed difference between the two arms, estimated from pilot reruns, and let $\delta$ be the minimum worthwhile gain the study predeclared. Under a normal approximation, @eq-paired-seed-count estimates the number of independent seed pairs needed to detect a mean difference of $\delta$ from zero:

$$n \approx \left(\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})\,\sigma_d}{\delta}\right)^2$$ {#eq-paired-seed-count}

Here $z_p$ is the $p$ quantile of a standard normal distribution. The significance level $\alpha$ limits false positives under the null hypothesis of no mean difference; $\beta$ is the probability of missing the specified difference, and $1-\beta$ is the test's power. For a two-sided $5\%$ test with $80\%$ power, the quantiles are approximately $1.96$ and $0.84$. Their squared sum is about eight, giving the planning rule $n \approx 8(\sigma_d/\delta)^2$ seed pairs, with one run from each arm in every pair.

If we seek a gain equal to the paired-difference dispersion, the rule gives on the order of eight pairs; a gain half that size requires about thirty. Smaller gains may demand more runs than the budget permits. These are approximate planning values, not guarantees, and $\sigma_d$ must come from the study's own pilot rather than another design's reported dispersion. Detecting a difference from zero also does not establish that it exceeds the minimum worthwhile gain; the final decision must compare the estimated effect and its uncertainty with that declared boundary. Bootstrap intervals, discussed below, describe uncertainty in the observed paired data. They do not automatically supply the same prospective sample-size calculation or compensate for too few independent observations.

The `pass@k` metric describes whether at least one out of $k$ generated candidates for a given task achieves a binary pass. When used, the report must specify the underlying estimator and sampling conventions [@Chen2021Codex; @JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. In hardware design, this metric requires a strict time or tool budget; finding a single success buried among dozens of expensive failures is often practically useless. Deployment reliability asks a different question: how often an ordinary run succeeds, not whether brute-forcing enough attempts eventually yields a winner. Neither score establishes physical validity beyond the narrow definition of the check used to define a pass.

Statistical analysis must align with both raw data and ultimate architectural claims. Nonparametric tests on paired observations require independent task units [@Demsar2006StatisticalComparisons]. Bootstrap intervals (drawing paired experimental units with replacement to estimate statistic variation [@EfronTibshirani1993Bootstrap]) summarize skewed statistics, but generating additional resamples never remedies a small, unrepresentative task set. Studies must report realized sample sizes, observed failures, effect sizes, calculated intervals, and the rationale behind analysis choices.

Studies claiming generalized performance across a broad task population must treat core architecture tasks as primary generalization units, pairing systems within specific tasks and conditions and treating repeated runs strictly as nested observations [@AgarwalEtAl2021StatisticalPrecipice]. A fixed benchmark suite or convenience sample supports nothing beyond the narrow population it represents. Per-task effects, uncertainty bounds, failure rates, and practical decision margins must be detailed, reporting an aggregate across-task effect only when the sampled task population justifies it. Exploratory tuning remains separated from held-out confirmation testing, declaring how evaluating multiple outcomes or subgroup comparisons impacts final decision rules.

### Robustness Across Churn and Dispersion

Evaluating workflow robustness in production environments requires moving beyond single-snapshot, peak-performance benchmarks. A design method that achieves a $15\%$ latency reduction on a static frozen benchmark but collapses when applied to everyday incremental code changes fails in real-world deployment. Evaluation must characterize the full distribution of candidate quality across multiple random seeds, prompt reformulations, and stochastic optimizer restarts. Metrics such as the interquartile range of achieved performance, the probability of generating physically invalid candidates, and worst-case regression bounds quantify whether an automated method is reliable enough for continuous deployment.

Evaluation benchmarks must also measure robustness to ongoing engineering changes. Feeding the design system a sequence of historical daily commits from an active production repository allows the benchmark to track *resynthesis latency*, the elapsed time required to restore validity after upstream software or RTL changes, alongside the compute cost of that work. It also measures *locality of invalidation* (whether the tool limits modifications to affected modules rather than changing previously verified subblocks) and the fraction of generated solutions that remain compatible with the updated mainline design.

### Operating Condition Sweeps and Claim Levels

Scaling studies must name the architectural difficulty axis under probe: total legal design-space size, number and coupling of constraints, tool-flow depth, feedback costs, or cross-layer span. Against the chosen axis, the report must document supported outcomes, failures, required human interventions, overall reliability, and total resource costs. Adjusting model sizes or task counts may serve as convenient experimental settings, but neither establishes that the core architectural problem became harder.

Sweeping operating conditions tests whether a complete-workflow advantage remains stable or collapses outside a narrow environment envelope; the condition-variation matrix declares which axes are swept and which are held fixed (@tbl-complete-workflow-condition-variation).

| **Factor family** | **Conditions to vary** | **Comparison basis held fixed** | **Question the variation answers** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workload and software | Input distribution, workload phase, compiler, runtime, and mapping | Architecture question, candidate identities, evaluator-owned checks, and total-cost rule | Does the complete-workflow advantage survive beyond a single workload or specialized software path? |
| Architecture and system | Interface traffic, memory hierarchy, synchronization, and energy assumptions | Required functions, declared objectives, workflow identities, and acceptance rules | Does the localized gain remain useful after representing surrounding system costs? |
| Implementation and tools | Fidelity stage, physical corner, tool version, configuration, and seed | RTL intent, acceptance properties, comparison arms, and resource-accounting window | Does the advantage survive higher-fidelity checks and inevitable apparatus variation? |
| Workflow configuration and information | Prompt or instruction policy, model or routing configuration, retrieval source, and represented-state freshness | Task population, legal actions, evaluator-owned tool access, checks, and reporting rules | Does the advantage depend entirely on one brittle configuration or a stale information state? |
: **Architecture-relevant variation tests the stability of measured complete-workflow advantages.** Each factor family either receives a matched test inside the declared population or remains an explicit, untested boundary. {#tbl-complete-workflow-condition-variation tbl-colwidths="[20,28,26,26]"}

When an observed advantage disappears under condition shifts, the tested envelope narrows accordingly. This matrix maps boundary conditions rather than pattern transferability, which is addressed in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack. A single isolated task cannot support a program-wide claim. An evaluation suite must span distinct architecture decisions, diverse workloads, varied designs, fluctuating result costs, multiple representations, different tool stages, and a wide range of failure consequences.

Results from these sweeps support claims at four levels, and the status a claim later earns cannot outrun the level its evidence reached: repeated runs on one task establish repeatability alone, meaning-preserving perturbations of encodings, seeds, spellings, and apparatus settings establish robustness, held-out tasks drawn from the declared population establish generalization within it, and a transfer claim to a new design family, toolchain, or process node needs a fresh target evaluation and recalibration there (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack).
